newsitem.title: FRANCE: Left catching up in latest French election poll.
newsitem.headline: Left catching up in latest French election poll.

text.p: French left-wing parties are catching up on the ruling centre-right majority according to the latest opinion poll released ahead of a May 25-June 1 general election.
The poll, released on Saturday, showed the left will win between 255 and 285 seats and the centre-right will get between 269 and 299 seats in the 577-member National Assembly.
The same poll conducted a week ago gave the left between 219 and 245 seats and the centre-right between 311 and 331 seats.
The extreme right-wing National Front would get up to two seats compared to up to three seats when the same poll was carried out last week. Ecologist groups would get no seats.
But 36 percent of voters said they could still change their minds, a high figure by French standards.
Both polls by the IFOP group appeared in the weekly newspaper Le Journal du Dimanche. The latest poll was conducted among 1,002 adults on Friday.
France's two-round electoral system favours established mainstream parties who can make between rounds agreements which exclude fringe and extremist groups from parliamentary life.

According to the poll, some 14 percent of voters will back the National Front in the first round compared to 16 percent a week earlier. Ecologist groups will get seven percent of the vote compared to 6.5 percent.
The Communist party, credited with 10 percent of voting intentions in the latest poll, would get between 23 and 29 seats. They were also credited with 10 percent last week.
But its uneasy ally the Socialist Party, with 28.5 percent of the vote, was projected to get nearly ten times more seats (232 to 256). The Socialists were credited with 26 percent last week.

The number of people who said they would vote for the two mainstream centre-right parties, the Gaullist Rally for the Republic (RPR) and the Union for French Democracy (UDF), stayed the same at 37 percent.
The above figures totalled 100 percent of those who answered the pollsters.

It did not include 22 percent (23 percent last week) of those polled who did not give their voting intention. Specialists sometimes say this group includes people who intend to vote for Communist or extreme-rightist candidates but decline to say so when polled.
